person.name: Andrew Honer
person.intro: I'm studying mechanical engineering at CU Boulder with a minor in physics. I enjoy CAD, reverse engineering, and hands-on projects, especially mechanical and automotive design.

projects.title: Nitecore NWL20
projects.subtitle: Reverse Engineering a Work Light
projects.summary: I disassembled and measured a Nitecore work light, then modeled its parts and assembly in SOLIDWORKS.
projects.lead: I wanted to understand how a work light’s housing, hinge, and internal components fit together.
projects.hero_alt: Andrew’s SOLIDWORKS model of the yellow and black Nitecore NWL20 in its upright position
projects.hero_caption: My assembled SOLIDWORKS model, shown in the upright configuration.
projects.note: Nitecore designed the original work light. I created the CAD model and drawings shown here.

sections.label: 01 / Overview
sections.title: Project Overview
paragraphs: I chose the NWL20 because I could take it apart and see how features like the magnetic base, 180-degree hinge, and carabiner were built. My goal was to recreate the parts and their assembly in SOLIDWORKS.

sections.label: 02 / Process
sections.title: Measurement & Modeling
paragraphs: I disassembled the light and measured the parts with calipers. I had to work around the circuit board and wires to reach some of the housing dimensions. I then put the modeled parts together in CAD to see how they fit.
sections.alt: Exploded SOLIDWORKS assembly showing the work light’s housing, lens, circuit board, battery, base and fasteners
sections.caption: The exploded assembly shows how the modeled components fit inside the housing.

sections.label: 03 / Challenges
sections.title: Modeling Challenges
paragraphs: The housing changes shape along its length and has very little symmetry. When I got stuck on a detail, I broke the shape down into simpler geometry and tried building it one feature at a time.

During development, I used the rollback bar to step back to an earlier point in the model. I also used feature suppression to temporarily take a modeling step out of the build. Both let me compare different ways to make a shape before choosing the approach I wanted to keep.

For the button on the outside of the housing, I used a fill pattern to repeat a detail within the button’s outline. I used draft cuts to recreate the slight taper on the housing. That angle gives an injection-molded part clearance as it comes out of the mold.

Several parts mount to the housing, so small measurement errors caused parts to overlap in the assembly. Where parts collided, I went back to the measurements and adjusted the dimensions of the mounting features.

pair.alt: Isometric CAD view of the work light’s black main housing and internal mounting features
pair.caption: Main housing: irregular geometry and several mounting interfaces.

pair.alt: Sectioned CAD model revealing the interior of the main housing
pair.caption: Section view: internal geometry that is hidden in the finished assembly.

sections.label: 04 / Documentation
sections.title: Engineering Drawings
paragraphs: I used detail views to enlarge small features so I could dimension them without crowding the main views. Section views showed the internal features and how the housing geometry changes through the part.
sections.alt: Engineering drawing of the main housing with multiple views, sections and dimensions
sections.caption: Engineering drawing of the main housing. Open the image to inspect the dimensions and views.

sections.label: 05 / Results
sections.title: Results & Lessons Learned
paragraphs: I modeled the buttons as part of the housing and left out the rubber seals and their grooves. The button pattern and material appearances also differ from the physical light. Those were limits of the model I documented alongside the assembly.

Trying different ways to build a feature took longer than I expected, and the drawings took about as much time as the modeling. I learned to budget time for both and decide which small details were worth modeling.

projects.title: Eagle Scout Service Project
projects.subtitle: A Shed and Accessible Sink for Animal Assisted Happiness
projects.summary: I planned and led a shed and accessible-sink project for Animal Assisted Happiness.
projects.lead: I led Scouts and adult volunteers in building a shed structure and replacing an outdoor sink at Animal Assisted Happiness.
projects.hero_alt: Andrew beside the finished shed at Animal Assisted Happiness
projects.hero_caption: The finished shed at Animal Assisted Happiness. My team built the floor, roof, and wall framing. The beneficiary finished the enclosure.

sections.label: 01 / Overview
sections.title: Project Overview
paragraphs: The farm needed a covered space for a washer and dryer to clean animal bedding and a handwashing station that people with disabilities could use. I drew the plans, researched materials and accessibility requirements, and set the budget.

pair.alt: The original outdoor area beside the red farm building before shed construction
pair.caption: Before construction: the outdoor area beside the farm building.

pair.alt: The installed accessible sink and countertop with open knee space underneath
pair.caption: The replacement sink and countertop provide an accessible handwashing location.

sections.label: 02 / Planning
sections.title: Planning & Design Changes
paragraphs: I first proposed an open shedrow with four posts and a roof for storage. When the farm asked for a laundry space, I revised the 8 × 10 ft plan to include a floor and framing for two walls. I updated the material list, cost estimate, and work schedule. I also used redwood and post-base brackets based on feedback about reducing the risk of rot.

sections.label: 03 / Construction
sections.title: Construction
paragraphs: I broke the revised build into stages. We marked and dug the post holes, leveled the brackets, and poured concrete before setting the posts and building the floor, wall framing, and roof. We also removed the old sink and installed the replacement sink, countertop, and supports.

I showed volunteers how to do their jobs and explained the hazards before they started. My plan called for a safety briefing each workday, closed-toe shoes, and a first-aid kit within reach. We planned for safety glasses, gloves, and hearing protection as needed and kept loose clothing and long hair clear of drills. I assigned cutting to adults and planned for Scouts to measure, dig, and drill under adult supervision.
sections.alt: The roofed timber shed structure during construction, before enclosure
sections.caption: The roof and framing before the shed was enclosed.

sections.label: 04 / Leadership
sections.title: Leadership & Challenges
paragraphs: The expanded scope gave me more jobs to coordinate. Early on, I had trouble stepping back and letting others do the work. As the build went on, I assigned jobs that could run at the same time and scheduled younger Scouts for days with work they could do. That helped me delegate individual tasks while keeping the whole workday moving.

sections.label: 05 / Results
sections.title: Results & Lessons Learned
paragraphs: My team completed the structural work and sink installation within the available funds and without injuries. The beneficiary finished the shed enclosure and connected the sink plumbing afterward.
Some jobs took longer than I estimated, so we stayed later to finish within the planned number of workdays. I learned to leave more room in the schedule for jobs that might take longer than expected.

projects.title: CU Autonomous Racing
projects.subtitle: Steering Design & Master Assembly
projects.summary: Completed kart chassis CAD for the master assembly, with steering design ongoing.
projects.lead: I work on the steering and master assembly subteams. We’re developing a go-kart that can steer under computer control.
projects.placeholder: Steering and vehicle integration are in development.

sections.label: 01 / Steering & Chassis
sections.title: CAD Work to Date
paragraphs: For our preliminary design review, I modeled a simplified pulley layout in Onshape. Our concept uses a 6 N·m stepper motor and a toothed belt, with a proposed 15-tooth motor pulley driving a 60-tooth pulley on the steering column. The larger pulley trades rotation speed for torque at the column.
I completed the reverse-engineered CAD model of the kart chassis. It gives the team a common reference for bringing each subteam’s parts into the master assembly.

sections.label: 02 / Next Steps
sections.title: Next Steps
paragraphs: We’re beginning force analysis to understand the loads on the steering system. We’ll use the results to guide the next design decisions as we develop the motor mount and finalize the belt and pulley layout.

projects.title: Approaching Vehicle Warning System
projects.subtitle: Wireless Distance Sensing & Driver Alerts
projects.summary: A two-device prototype that estimates closing speed and warns the driver through an OLED display and speaker.
projects.lead: I led software development, integration, and troubleshooting for our team’s wireless rear-approach warning prototype.

sections.label: 01 / Problem & Objectives
sections.title: Problem & Design Objectives
paragraphs: Drivers may miss a vehicle approaching quickly from behind. We developed an aftermarket warning-system prototype to help drivers recognize rapidly approaching or excessively close objects behind their vehicle.

The project started with left-lane driving behavior, then broadened into a rear-approach warning system. We aimed for consistent measurements, reliable warnings, affordable components, straightforward installation, and minimal interference with normal driving.

sections.label: 02 / System Design
sections.title: System Design
paragraphs: The prototype has two wireless devices in custom 3D-printed enclosures. At the rear of the vehicle, an Arduino reads a LiDARLite v3 sensor and sends distance measurements over long-range nRF24L01 radios to a second Arduino inside the car.

The receiver estimates relative closing speed from successive distance readings. A rolling average smooths fluctuations. An approximately 2-inch OLED normally shows distance and closing speed. If an object approaches too quickly or becomes too close, the display shows a warning and an MP3 audio module drives a speaker.
We began with an ultrasonic sensor, then moved to LiDAR for longer-distance measurements. The team also upgraded the radios, display, and speaker as the prototype developed.

equation.description: d₁ and d₂ are successive distance readings, separated by the elapsed time Δt. Positive v indicates an object closing the gap.

pair.caption: The receiver displaying distance and estimated closing speed inside the car.

pair.caption: The approaching-fast warning interface during a prototype demonstration.

sections.label: 03 / My Contributions
sections.title: Individual Contributions
paragraphs: I handled nearly all software development and iteration. I defined the system’s behavior, configured the wireless link, processed LiDAR measurements, and implemented closing-speed calculations and rolling-average filtering.

I developed the warning logic for fast approaches and nearby objects, integrated the OLED interface and audible alerts, and adjusted audio timing. Much of the work involved getting the software and physical electronics to behave consistently together.
I also adjusted tolerances on an existing enclosure design before printing. The hardware, electronics, and enclosure work were shared team efforts.

subsections.title: Isolating a Wireless Failure
paragraphs: When the radios stopped communicating reliably, I first suspected the software. I reduced it to minimal transmitter and receiver test programs, swapped modules between Arduino boards, and isolated possible hardware causes. I eventually traced the failure to a faulty ground connection. Testing the simplest working setup helped me separate the connection problem from the application code.

subsections.title: Stabilizing Readings & Warnings
paragraphs: Early versions produced inconsistent closing-speed estimates, invalid distances, and unintended warnings. I revised measurement processing, the rolling average, and warning logic through repeated tests. I also worked on playback timing so audible warnings would play at the appropriate point.

subsections.title: Fitting the Final Electronics
paragraphs: The team tried several displays before settling on the larger OLED. The enclosure designs changed to fit the final electronics and a larger speaker. I refined the enclosure tolerances before printing.

sections.label: 05 / Testing & Results
sections.title: Testing & Results
paragraphs: We installed the prototype on my Mini Cooper Clubman and confirmed that the rear module could communicate with the interior receiver through the vehicle. In controlled tests, people walked and ran toward the sensor. We demonstrated both fast-approach and too-close warnings, and distance readings reached approximately 128 feet.

These demonstrations showed the prototype operating in its intended mounting configuration. Testing with moving vehicles remains future work, along with the accuracy and reliability evaluation needed for an automotive safety application.
The final expo poster listed $242 in hardware, including a $150 LiDAR sensor borrowed from the ITLL. The other listed components total $92. These figures describe the poster’s component budget.
sections.alt: Completed sensor and receiver devices with the final blue expo poster and demonstration screens
sections.caption: Our expo display with both completed devices, the final blue poster, and demonstration screens.

sections.label: 06 / Lessons & Next Steps
sections.title: Reflection & Future Work
paragraphs: I came into this project with programming and CAD experience, but working with physical electronics made me pay more attention to how the hardware and software affected each other. The ground-connection problem taught me to isolate variables and test components independently before changing the larger program.

I would order components and test the basic system earlier next time. We spent time refining enclosures before confirming that the parts inside them would work. That made later hardware changes more time-consuming.
Future ideas include camera-based vehicle identification, smaller enclosures, improved mounts, and controlled tests with moving vehicles.

sections.label: 07 / Expo & Recognition
sections.title: Expo & Recognition
paragraphs: We presented a working prototype at CU Boulder’s November 14, 2026 Engineering Projects Expo and received the APEX Innovation Award from the CU Racing Team.
Our five-person team, Big Kahunas, included Atahan Tosun, Carter Jenson, Andrew Honer, Jason Schwartz, and Ved Kadam. The course was taught by Professor Dan Godrick.
